summary: Intro + qualification for Redwood PLG quickstart. Solaris AI evaluating hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for customer-facing summarization API. Discussed free credits, time-to-first-token, benchmarks, security (SOC2, KMS, SSO), and pilot scope. Agreed next steps: send quickstart and security materials, run initial benchmark, schedule pilot kickoff.
topics: Redwood PLG quickstart / free credits / onboarding
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
transcript: [00:00] Alex Rivera: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE for the account. Sam from our SE team is with me. How's everyone doing?

[00:08] Jordan Miles: Good, thanks. Jordan here. We have Priya and Liam on as well. We're mainly trying to understand how fast we can get from sign-up to a usable API for customers, and what the migration path looks like if we need Dedicated or Private later.

[00:20] Alex Rivera: Totally, that's the exact thing we try to make frictionless with the PLG quickstart. We'll cover free credits, SDKs, and rough time-to-first-token. Sam can jump into performance implications. Quick question first: what's your current stack and where will the model run today?

[00:32] Priya Kapoor: We're currently using a mix; for prototyping we use OpenAI for summarization features, but we want more control and better unit economics. Production is on GCP. Main constraints: latency under 400ms for 90th pct, PCI-sensitive data for a subset of customers, and audit logging needs.
[00:50] Sam Chen: Got it. When you say 400ms 90th, is that end-to-end from your app to token response or just model token generation?
[00:58] Liam O'Neal: End-to-end. Our front-end waits for the chunked summary to start. Ideally streaming start <250ms for small requests, full response under 400ms.

[01:10] Alex Rivera: Makes sense. For the quickstart hosted API you can usually get a basic integration and first token in under 10-15 minutes — sign up, apply credits, create an API key, and call the text-generation endpoint. Streaming support is available in the SDKs. Dedicated will give you predictable throughput for high-QPS workloads but takes some lead time to provision.
[01:30] Jordan Miles: How long does Dedicated provisioning take? We're trying to map timelines — if we like hosted and traffic grows, can we switch without rewriting prompts or client code?

[01:40] Sam Chen: Yes, that's one of our design goals. The API surface stays the same. Dedicated provisioning is typically a few days to a couple weeks depending on capacity and region, plus an onboarding window. The migration is mostly config: changing endpoint/credentials and optionally model pinning. Some customers do a canary on Dedicated to validate latency/costs.
[01:58] Priya Kapoor: And Private deployment? We have a few regulated customers that might require VPC or on-prem in the future.

[02:05] Sam Chen: We offer a Private option for VPC or on-prem installs. That has a longer lead time, more infra work, and license terms. For discovery you're right to start hosted quickstart while evaluating pilot benchmarks for Dedicated/Private.
[02:25] Jordan Miles: Security is big for us — SOC2, SSO, KMS. Can you outline what the hosted default provides and where Dedicated/Private differs?

[02:34] Alex Rivera: Hosted comes with SOC2 compliance, encryption at rest and in transit, and we support customer-managed KMS for Dedicated and Private. For SSO we have SAML/SSO integrations, RBAC in the Console, and audit logs. We'll send the security whitepaper and SOC2 report after this call.
[02:50] Liam O'Neal: Do you have details on data retention and redaction in hosted? For some customers we need to ensure raw inputs aren't persisted longer than X days.

[02:58] Sam Chen: We have configurable retention policies; hosted defaults to 30 days for logs but can be adjusted under contract for Dedicated/Private. We'll include the specific retention controls in the docs Sam will share.

[03:15] Alex Rivera: Quick note on pricing/credits: the PLG quickstart includes free credits for you to run a pilot. It covers a set amount of tokens and is intended for proof-of-concept. After credits you can continue on pay-as-you-go or move to reserved capacity for better unit economics.
[03:30] Priya Kapoor: What about latency/cost tradeoffs — quantized models, batching, or KV cache? We saw mentions of KV caches in your docs but not sure when they'd help.

[03:40] Sam Chen: Batching reduces token cost by increasing throughput but can add latency; continuous prefix/KV cache helps for repeated contexts and can significantly reduce compute for conversational patterns. Quantized models (4-bit/8-bit) also reduce cost with some quality tradeoffs. For your use case, short summaries, caching repeated prompts and using a low-latency model variant is usually best.
[04:02] Jordan Miles: Can we run a quick benchmark as part of the pilot? We want to measure p95 latency and token cost across 1000 sample requests.

[04:10] Alex Rivera: Absolutely. Sam will share a benchmark spreadsheet and suggested prompt set. Typical pilot includes 1k requests across short and long inputs, comparing hosted (standard) vs hosted with caching vs Dedicated pinned model.
[04:25] Priya Kapoor: Onboarding — what's the time-to-first-token again? We want to set expectations for internal stakeholders.

[04:30] Alex Rivera: For PLG quickstart it's minutes for a basic call, and about 1-2 days for a production-ready integration with streaming and retries configured. We'll make sure the quickstart guide walks you through SDK examples and a one-file curl test so your engineers get tokens fast.
[04:48] Liam O'Neal: Any gotchas around network egress or regional endpoints? We host in GCP but need EU residency for some customers.

[04:55] Sam Chen: We have regions in NA and EU; you can route by region. For EU residency we can provision Dedicated in EU or discuss Private with in-region deployment. There are egress cost considerations but that's more on infra side; we'll share region options in the doc.
[05:12] Jordan Miles: Ok. For the quickstart, what credentials do we need to get going? Our security folks will ask about API key rotation and audit log access.

[05:18] Alex Rivera: You'll create a service API key in the Console; keys can be rotated and scoped. Audit logs are available in the Console and via streaming to your SIEM for Dedicated/Private as well. We'll include key rotation best practices in the guide.
[05:32] Priya Kapoor: Does the quickstart include a sandbox model catalog or is it the same models as production?
[05:37] Sam Chen: Same models — but we offer small compute variants for quick tests and recommended config profiles. For production you can pin model versions to prevent drift.
[05:47] Jordan Miles: Any mention of hallucination controls or eval tooling? We need to track quality regression over time.

[05:54] Alex Rivera: Yes, Redwood Optimize includes evaluation hooks and regression alerts tied to prompt sets. In the quickstart we'll show a basic eval harness for your prompt set so you can monitor quality across releases.
[06:08] Liam O'Neal: That sounds good. On the integration side — SDKs in Node and Python? We prefer Python for back-end processes.
[06:14] Sam Chen: Node, Python, and a simple curl example. We'll send sample code tailored to summarization streaming which matches your stack.
[06:22] Jordan Miles: If we hit a privacy requirement and need Private on-prem later, how much code change?

[06:28] Sam Chen: Minimal. The API is consistent. Most work is infra and keys. You may need to adjust network peering and storage integrations. We'll map that in the pilot plan so you can estimate migration costs.
[06:40] Priya Kapoor: Can you share a few reference customers in regulated spaces? Hearing real examples helps our security review.
[06:46] Alex Rivera: Yes, we can share anonymized references and vertical case studies — we'll include a couple in the follow-up email.
[06:55] Jordan Miles: On pricing after credits: do you offer committed reserved capacity for lower unit cost?

[07:02] Alex Rivera: Yes — Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly/annual commits and better unit costs. We also offer burst policies and autoscaling. For initial pilots, most teams start hosted then evaluate reserved commits after they hit predictable throughput.
[07:18] Liam O'Neal: Are there SDKs or tooling for cost monitoring and token breakdowns? We want to instrument cost per feature.
[07:25] Sam Chen: Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and tracing. You can also export usage to your billing system.
[07:36] Priya Kapoor: A quick technical question: how do you handle KV cache invalidation for ephemeral contexts? We have sessions that expire quickly.
[07:44] Sam Chen: Cache TTLs are configurable per route; you can set per-session TTL or explicitly evict. We'll include configuration examples in the docs.

[07:56] Jordan Miles: Ok, let's talk success criteria. For us to move from pilot to production we need: 1) p95 latency <400ms, 2) token cost be competitive with current provider, 3) SOC2 and KMS controls verified, 4) migration path for Dedicated or Private. Does that sound right?
[08:14] Alex Rivera: That's perfect. We'll structure the pilot to validate those four buckets. Sam will help design the benchmark and we'll provide an acceptance checklist.
[08:25] Priya Kapoor: One more on SSO: we use Okta. Any gotchas with SAML integrations?
[08:31] Sam Chen: Standard SAML flow, Okta is common. Our CIAM docs show steps; for Dedicated/Private we can do SCIM provisioning as well.
[08:40] Jordan Miles: Good. Can you outline the timelines again: quickstart -> bench -> pilot -> Dedicated?

[08:45] Alex Rivera: Quickstart and initial bench: 1 week using free credits. Pilot kickoff and run: 2-4 weeks depending on scope. Dedicated provisioning: a few days to a couple weeks once contract and capacity are in place. Private on-prem longer and we'll estimate it once we see the pilot requirements.
[09:00] Priya Kapoor: Let's confirm the free credits amount and how to redeem them. Our legal needs to approve any T&Cs before we transfer data into the service for the pilot.

[09:07] Alex Rivera: We'll include the redemption instructions in the follow-up email and attach the standard T&Cs. For pilot data you can use masked/anonymized sets until legal signs off; that is a common approach.
[09:20] Jordan Miles: Any technical deep dive items we should prepare for the pilot kickoff?

[09:24] Sam Chen: We should gather your sample prompt set, a representative dataset for summarization, expected QPS, and the acceptance thresholds. Also share any network constraints or IP allowlists so we can plan endpoints.

[09:36] Alex Rivera: Quick recap and next steps in the last 2 minutes. We'll send a follow-up with: quickstart guide and free credits, benchmark spreadsheet, SOC2/KMS whitepaper, suggested prompts, and proposed pilot schedule. You confirm dataset and availability and we'll lock in pilot kickoff.
[09:54] Jordan Miles: Sounds good. Priya or Liam, anything else?
[09:58] Priya Kapoor: No that's it from Product. Liam will prep the dataset and prompts.
[10:04] Liam O'Neal: I'll get the 1k sample requests and a few longer examples ready. Expect an email by Friday.
[10:12] Alex Rivera: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with materials by tomorrow EOD. Meeting adjourned.
[10:18] -- End of recording --
